Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 45
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Chef
  trauma_type: Rape
  pcl5: 70

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily., Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order, Blocked Before Complete: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it
  Negative Appraisals: No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened, Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma

Vignette:
Sione was forty-five when he walked into the intake room, but the story still rested heavily in his chest like the week he turned twenty-eight and the restaurant closed at two in the morning. He had been clearing a private dining hall for a corporate event when a guest he had served drinks to followed him into the narrow corridor behind the walk-in cooler. The space was tight, the air thick with the hum of refrigeration units and the lingering scent of roasted garlic. What frightened Sione most was the sudden shift in his body: one moment he was steering, the next he was pinned against the stainless-steel shelving, the weight of another man pressing him down while his arms were held wide. He can talk about what happened very easily, and on the drive over he had repeated the account without hesitation, yet inside his head the memories of the event did not line up. Sometimes the click of the guest’s belt comes first; sometimes the warmth of the garlic air rises before the pressure on his wrists. He finds himself pushing the memory away before he can fully recall it, stepping back just as the picture sharpens, letting the edges blur so the moment does not catch him. Over the weeks and months that followed, Sione had come to believe he was no longer capable of doing the things that defined him. The kitchen, once his domain, grew heavy alongside the tightness in his shoulders. He could still talk about the event, but the daily rhythm of the line felt unfamiliar. He started avoiding the narrow corridor where the encounter took place, and when colleagues reached toward him from behind during the rush, he would flinch and step backward. The feeling of being contaminated settled over him. He felt dirty even after scrubbing his hands at the pot sink, and the residue lingered in his awareness parallel to the heavy sense that his life had been destroyed. His life was no longer the continuous path he had imagined; his marriage ended that winter, and he stopped seeing the way his former wife’s hands had rested on his shoulders, interpreting the touch as another weight he could no longer bear. The memories, the contamination, the sense of lost capability, and the unraveling of his personal world existed side by side in his kitchen, each occupying its own space without demanding explanation from the others. The restaurant where Sione works as a chef became the ground where these patterns took root. During the evening service, when the doors swung open and staff clustered in the pass, he would watch the hands reaching for plates, for knives, for each other, and feel the familiar tightness in his chest. He began taking prep shifts in the back, where the space was wider and the air circled more freely, while the work grew heavier. He lost the authority he once held, while his skills remained steady, and his trust in the daily motion shifted alongside the heavy feeling in his chest. The avoidance formed quietly at first—a shifted station, a declined promotion, a hesitation before stepping into the walk-in cooler—and then it compounded into a quiet exile from the rhythm he had known for years. A PCL5 score of seventy now maps the weight he has been carrying, reflecting the days when the blurred sequence of memory makes him second-guess every reach and every step. Now, Sione sits in the clinic with the PCL5 score tracking the days he has carried this weight. He does not fear the memory itself so much as the moment before it arrives, when he can feel it pressing against the surface of his mind. What he hopes for is not to erase the story, but to let it settle in its proper place without pulling him backward. He is tired of the residue, tired of the confused sequence that makes the kitchen feel like a room of overlapping moments, and he has come to the clinic because the line is no longer a place he can inhabit without bracing himself. He knows he can speak of what happened, but he wants to find a way to stand in the heat of the service, to let his hands work without the tightness of being held, and to stop feeling that his life is still caught in that narrow corridor behind the cooler.
